summary: Evolves the Interfaces group of MIB-II, describing managed objects for network interfaces so SNMP can show their state and traffic. It was replaced by RFC 2233.

eli5.summary: Every network plug on a computer can be listed with its status. This memo updates the list.

questions: what is the interfaces group mib
subtitle: How SNMP describes network interfaces: sub-layers, stable indexes, 64-bit counters and better status reporting.

tldr.problem: The MIB-II interfaces group assumed one simple row per interface. Experience with media-specific MIBs showed it could not describe stacked sub-layers, dynamic interfaces, virtual circuits, fast media whose 32-bit counters wrap quickly, or speeds above ifSpeed's range.
tldr.mechanism: The memo gives each sub-layer its own ifTable row and links them with a new ifStackTable. It also relaxes ifIndex numbering, adds ifName, 64-bit high-capacity counters, ifHighSpeed, a dormant state and trap control, and re-specifies the group in SNMPv2 form.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1573 became the reference for evolving the interfaces group and incorporated RFC 1229. It has been obsoleted by RFC 2233.

today: RFC 1573 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 2233. It obsoleted RFC 1229, so refer to RFC 2233 for the current definition of the interfaces group.

sections.title: Why the Interfaces Group Needed to Evolve
sections.content:
This memo defines managed objects for network interfaces in the Management Information Base (MIB) used with network management protocols. It revisits the interfaces group of MIB-II, which gives a generic set of objects so any network interface can be managed in an interface-independent way, with media-specific MIB modules (for example for Ethernet) as extensions.

Many media-specific MIB modules have been written since MIB-II was standardized. The experience showed that the MIB-II model is too simplistic or static for some of them, and some modules had already loosened it. The memo documents and standardizes that evolution and fills the resulting gaps. It also applies the earlier extensions of RFC 1229 and thereby incorporates them.

The memo includes a MIB module that re-specifies the interfaces group in a form that complies with the SNMPv2 SMI and is semantically identical to the existing SNMPv1-based definitions. Section 3 lists nine problem areas: interface numbering, sub-layers, virtual circuits, bit, character and fixed-length interfaces, counter size, interface speed, multicast and broadcast counters, new ifType values, and ifSpecific.
sections.eli5: The old list of network plugs assumed each plug was one simple thing. New gear has plugs built from several layers, so the list needed better rules.

sections.title: Sub-Layers and the ifStackTable
sections.content:
Network interfaces are often built from several sub-layers, each with its own media-specific MIB, such as PPP running over an HDLC link on an RS232-like connector. MIB-II's single row per interface, with one ifType value, cannot describe this, and it cannot describe multiplexing either. In upward multiplexing, such as MLP, several serial lines appear as one point-to-point link. In downward multiplexing, several PPP instances run over one T1 channel.

The memo considered two alternatives that keep one row for the whole interface and rejected both, because they need pointers in every media-specific MIB or cannot handle PPP over MLP, and both require an ifType value for every combination. The adopted solution is one ifTable row per sub-layer, plus a new ifStackTable that identifies the superior and subordinate sub-layers using INTEGER pointers to ifTable rows. This supports both kinds of multiplexing and needs an ifType value only for each sub-layer.

Packet counters are defined as counting packets delivered to, or requested by, a "higher-layer", which can be a bridge's forwarding module, a higher sub-layer, or the local IP module. For virtual circuits, the memo strongly recommends not giving each circuit its own ifTable row, though a media-specific MIB may do so if it explains why.
sections.eli5: A plug can be made of several pieces stacked up, like a cable, an adapter and a converter. Instead of one row for the whole stack, each piece gets its own row and a second list says which piece sits on top of which.

sections.title: Numbering, Tables and Object Groups
sections.content:
MIB-II said ifIndex ranges between 1 and ifNumber, which clashes with interfaces being added and removed dynamically. The memo drops the requirement that ifIndex be less than ifNumber, and keeps ifNumber as the count of rows. After an interface is dynamically removed, its ifIndex MUST NOT be reused by a different interface until the next re-initialization of the network management system. It recommends that values still be small integers starting at 1, even if there are holes. A new InterfaceIndex textual convention carries the semantics of ifIndex for other MIB modules.

Since index values no longer map neatly to physical ports, a new object, ifName, holds the device's own name for the interface, for example wan1. ifSpecific is deprecated. The ifType enumeration moves into the IANAifType textual convention so IANA can add values without a new RFC.

The MIB has five tables: ifTable, ifXTable (new and replacement objects), ifStackTable, ifTestTable and ifRcvAddressTable. Object groups define which objects apply to which kind of interface: ifGeneralGroup for all, ifPacketGroup for packet-oriented ones, and ifFixedLengthGroup for character-oriented and fixed-length ones such as cell relay. The memo requires media-specific MIB designers to specify their layering model and say how virtual circuits, ifTestTable and ifRcvAddressTable apply.
sections.eli5: Each plug keeps its number for good, even if neighbours are unplugged, and now also has a name like wan1 that people can understand.

sections.title: Counters and Speed on Fast Links
sections.content:
As media get faster, 32-bit counters wrap sooner. Back-to-back full-size packets wrap ifInOctets in just over 57 minutes on Ethernet, 36 minutes on 16 megabit Token Ring, 12 minutes on a US T3 line and 5.7 minutes on FDDI. The memo rejected scaling the counters because slow interfaces would then look bursty, and instead adds 64-bit high capacity counters in the ifHCFixedLengthGroup, ifHCPacketGroup and ifVHCPacketGroup.

The 32-bit counters are not deprecated and MUST still be available, reporting the low 32 bits of the 64-bit count. Which to use depends on speed: 32-bit counters MUST be used at 20,000,000 bits per second or less. Between that and 650,000,000, 32-bit packet counters and 64-bit octet counters MUST be used. At 650,000,000 or faster, both packet and octet counters MUST be 64-bit.

ifSpeed can report at most (231)-1 bits per second, so a new ifHighSpeed reports speed in units of 1,000,000 bits per second. The non-unicast packet counters are deprecated in favour of separate multicast and broadcast counters.
sections.eli5: A car's odometer that only has a few digits flips back to zero quickly on a very fast car. The fix is to give the fast cars a longer odometer.

sections.title: Interface Status and Traps
sections.content:
Because each sub-layer has a row, each can generate linkUp and linkDown traps, so one event could yield several. A new ifLinkUpDownTrapEnable object lets a manager limit traps, and by default only the lowest sub-layer of an interface generates them.

ifOperStatus gains a dormant state for an interface that is operable but waiting for an external event, as with an on-demand dial-up link. When ifAdminStatus is not down and ifOperStatus is down, a fault is presumed. If ifAdminStatus is down, ifOperStatus normally goes down too, perhaps after a short lag; a manager that sees a mismatch should wait and check again before raising an error.

When ifAdminStatus goes up, ifOperStatus becomes up only if packets can be sent and received, dormant if waiting, down on a fault, unknown if the state cannot be found out, or testing if tests must run. The memo defines traps in terms of transitions into and out of the down state, because those are most useful to managers and match current usage. Its Security Considerations section says security issues are not discussed.
sections.eli5: A plug can now say "I am asleep and waiting for someone to call" instead of just on or off. Only the bottom piece of the stack rings the alarm bell by default, so you hear one bell rather than many.
